transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
New Jersey Governor Mike E. Sherrill has declared a state of emergency for the state's coastal
communities.
A nor'easter is bringing high winds, heavy rains, and large waves to the region.
In declaring the emergency, Sherrill urged people to take the storm seriously and stay
alert.
With this state of emergency, what that means is we will surge resources to these communities,
making sure that the Department of Environmental Protection, the Department of Transportation,
are manning our operation centers because of beach erosion and the high tide and the
roads that we are concerned about.
Thousands of people are now without power in the region, while roads are flooding in
some coastal New Jersey communities.
Hurricane Nolo has Hawaii's Big Island in its sights.
The National Weather Service says tropical storm conditions are expected late tonight,
with winds gusting to 50 miles an hour and as much as 10 to 15 inches of rain.
And Hurricane Polo is now a Category 5 storm, and is expected to make landfall in the Baja
California peninsula.
The Supreme Court has for now revived a federal data system the Trump administration revamped
into a tool to check the citizenship of millions of registered voters.
As NPR's Jude Joffee Block reports, the tool had been used by some states before it was
blocked by a federal judge for violating privacy protections.
The federal tool is called SAVE, and the Trump administration made major changes to it last
year, including linking it to social security data for the first time.
But the tool has mistakenly flagged some U.S. citizens as potential non-citizens, leading
them to be taken off state voter rolls as a result.
A federal judge in June said the modified version of SAVE trampled on the privacy rights
of Americans and threatened the right to vote.
But the Supreme Court lifted that block and opened the door for the new SAVE tool to be
used in the lead-up to the election for individualized determinations of citizenship.
The law bars systematic purges of voter rolls this close to an election.
Jude Joffee Block, NPR News.
Israel has closed several of its military checkpoints in the occupied West Bank.
The move caused traffic jams for Palestinians.
This comes ahead of Israel's national election, says NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells us.
Ali Hussein Yusuf Abdullah was trying to cross one checkpoint near Ramallah on foot in hopes
of visiting his sick aunt.
He said he'd been waiting more than two hours when he talked with NPR's producer in the
West Bank, Nuhamusleh, who said dozens of cars were backed up at the crossing for hours.
The further limiting of movement comes after a Palestinian car-ramming attack seriously
wounded an Israeli soldier, the son of Israel's ambassador to the U.S.
Days earlier, a Palestinian gunman killed an Israeli settler, while there has been a wave
of settler violence against Palestinians.
Meanwhile, Israel has ramped up its military presence in the occupied territory, fearing
an explosion of violence as Election Day draws closer.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
And you're listening to NPR News.
Iran says it will reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program, but
only if the U.S. implements several conditions over the next seven days.
Those conditions include the U.S. lifting its naval blockade of Iran's ports, agreeing
to a ceasefire that includes Lebanon and waving sanctions in Iranian oil sales.
Iran's foreign minister announced the proposal Friday outside the U.N. Security Council.
Investors bought stocks and dumped bonds this week, as NPR's Scott Horsley reports, a sell-off
in the bond market pushed mortgage rates to their highest level since the beginning of
last year.
Long-term Treasury yields jumped again this week, as investors demand a bigger return
to lend money for the government in the face of stubborn inflation.
The yield on 10-year Treasuries climbed to the highest level in two decades.
Average mortgage rates, which tend to follow Treasury yields, rose to just over 7 percent.
Mortgage rates had briefly dropped below 6 percent just before the U.S. launched its war
with Iran and triggered a spike in energy prices.
Today's higher borrowing costs have been a drag on the housing market.
Sales of existing homes in August were the slowest in more than a year.
For the week, the Dow Jones industrial average rose three-tenths of a percent, the S&P 500
index climbed 1.2 percent, and the Nasdaq jumped more than 2 percent.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
The Irish band U2 was back in Dublin Friday, where they performed for students at Mount
Temple Comprehensive School, where the band was formed 50 years ago.
Lead singer Bono thanked the school and surrounding community for its support of the band over
the years.
The seven-song set they played was a promotion for the band's newest album, which will be
released in mid-November.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
